vignette:
Emily is a 30-year-old married bank teller who came to treatment after months of telling herself she should be able to handle things on her own. During the first meetings, she described the traumatic event carefully at first and then in fragments, because whenever she got too close to it she became flooded and had to stop. What happened to her was torture. She spoke about being held in a confined place where other people controlled when she could move, where she was watched continuously, and where fear was used deliberately against her. She remembered the atmosphere as much as any single act: the feeling of eyes on her, the unbearable anticipation when everything suddenly went quiet, and the moments when anger in someone else's face or voice meant something terrible might happen next. She also described sexual violation as part of what she endured, so that intimacy later came to carry the same sense of danger rather than comfort.

In the weeks after, Emily found that the memories did not stay in the past. They returned without warning, set off by things around her before she had time to prepare herself. At work at the bank, if a customer's expression hardened or a voice became tense even without shouting, her body reacted immediately. She would feel as if she were back there, not just remembering but reliving it across all her senses at once. The look on a face, the sense of being observed from across the counter, even a quiet pause in the lobby before the next customer stepped forward could bring it on. She said that when the memory came back, it was "all of it at once," so vivid and complete that she could not hold on to the fact that she was standing in her branch in daylight, wearing her name tag, with coworkers nearby. What frightened her was how suddenly it happened. She could be counting bills one second and then feel plunged into the event with no warning.

Because of that, Emily began moving through the world as if danger might announce itself in subtle ways. Unusual silence was especially hard for her. If the house became too quiet at night, she became certain something was wrong and would wake fully alert, checking doors, windows, and the rooms around her before she could settle again. Small noises startled her easily, and she noticed how quickly her shoulders jumped or her heart pounded when someone approached unexpectedly. She tried to explain to her husband that what disturbed her was not only noise, but silence itself, the kind of silence that to her felt loaded, as if something harmful were just about to happen.

Over time she changed how she dealt with other people. At the bank she kept her gaze lowered and avoided eye contact with customers and coworkers as much as she could. Looking directly at someone made her feel exposed, too visible, too much as though she were once again under scrutiny. This affected her work in concrete ways. Customers sometimes read her as cold or distracted, and she worried about making mistakes because so much effort went into getting through each interaction. At home, intimacy with her husband became difficult. Sexual situations brought up immediate dread and a felt sense of threat. She was not describing a loss of affection for him; rather, her body reacted as though closeness itself were unsafe. She often withdrew without being able to explain fully, and the distance between them had become one of the things that finally convinced her she needed help.

Emily also spent long stretches of time going over the event in her mind, trying to make sense of every detail. She revisited what happened repeatedly, as if there might be some arrangement of the facts that would make it feel understandable or controllable. Yet when the memory became too vivid, she had to break off because the emotional force of it was overwhelming. Alongside this, she found herself spending money impulsively, especially after difficult shifts or bad nights. She described buying things online or stopping at stores not because she needed anything, but because for a brief period it distracted and soothed her. The relief never lasted, and afterward she felt embarrassed and more strained, especially as the purchases accumulated.

By the time she sought treatment, Emily felt hemmed in by her own reactions. She was exhausted from waking in the night to make sure she was safe, tense at work whenever she felt watched, and increasingly distressed by how intimacy with her husband had become tied to alarm. What finally brought her in was a recent day at the bank when a customer's controlled, angry expression instantly threw her into a full reliving of the trauma, leaving her shaken in front of colleagues. She said she was afraid of what it meant that ordinary moments could disappear so suddenly into the past, and she was hoping, cautiously, that treatment might help her feel present in her own life again.
